title: Leading around a known void

feedback.title: Leading your ace into a known void
feedback.summary: You lead this trick, and West acts last in it. The earlier trick shows West already void in Clubs, so leading the ace of Clubs offers West a free chance to trump it with any Heart.
points: The earlier trick shows West playing a Heart when Clubs were led, so West holds no more Clubs this hand.
West acts last in this new trick too, so nothing you lead is safe from a seat you already know is void in it, if West chooses to trump.
A different lead avoids this specific, already-confirmed exposure; the ace is not required to win this trick to make progress elsewhere.

feedback.title: Avoid the one confirmed risk on the table
feedback.summary: Leading Diamonds instead avoids West's known Club void entirely. Nothing shown here confirms Diamonds carry any comparable exposure.
points: West's void is specifically in Clubs; leading a different suit does not hand West a free, already-confirmed opportunity to trump.
This does not prove Diamonds are safe in every sense — no evidence about Diamonds is shown either way — only that the one identified risk is avoided.
The ace of Clubs is not spent here; it remains available for a later trick where the known void does not apply.

author_notes: EC-055 checkpoint-3 coverage: a fifth void-tracking scenario, and the first where South leads (current_trick is empty) rather than responds. play_void_tracking_001/002/004 are all about playing into an already-started trick; the tactical question here is different in kind: which suit to lead, given a known void for the seat that will act last in the new trick. Rotation from South leading is South-East-North-West, so West (the known void seat) is last to act, mirroring the structural risk in play_void_tracking_001 but at the leading decision rather than the following one. No claim is made that Diamonds are safe beyond the absence of contrary evidence.
